Five retained techniques and final source code

These techniques form one measured configuration. Their gains are not additive. Code fragments use the surrounding kernel variables.

Reload low K bands

Load K rows 0–127 from the existing LDS buffer when dQ needs them.

if FRAGMENT_CHAIN and N == 8192:
    k_resident_lo = None
else:
    k_resident_lo = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(k_buffer, [0, 0], [128, D]), token=initial_wait,
                                   layout=k_md_layout, relaxed=True)

if k_resident_lo is None:
    k0 = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(k_buffer, [0, 0], [32, 128]), layout=K_MD_LAYOUT, relaxed=True,
                        rematerialize_coordinates_group=COORDINATE_GROUP)
else:
    k0 = tlx.extract_slice(k_resident_lo, [32, 128], [0, 0])

Open final kernel source

Use native LSE scaling

Keep FP32 multiplication visible to LLVM. The empty scalar pin contains no instruction.

lse_log2 = tl.inline_asm_elementwise(
    "",
    "=v,0",
    [lse_values * 1.4426950408889634],
    dtype=tl.float32,
    is_pure=True,
    pack=1,
)

Open final kernel source

Pin the front in four-register groups

Pin scores and dP to VGPRs in groups of four registers.

GQA8K_FRONT_REGISTERS_PER_GROUP: tl.constexpr = 4

if PIN_FRONT:
    scores = tlx.amd_register_resident(
        scores,
        register_class="vgpr",
        registers_per_group=GQA8K_FRONT_REGISTERS_PER_GROUP if GQA8K_FRONT else 16,
    )

Open final kernel source

Delay the Q RHS load

Place a scheduling marker after the front. It adds no hardware synchronization.

if FRAGMENT_CHAIN and N == 8192:
    tlx.amd_sched_barrier(0)

Open final kernel source

Select reverse register assignment

Enable this default only for the measured GQA8K shape. Explicit environment overrides remain active.

measured_gqa8k = shape == (16, 64, 8, 8192, 128) and not causal and split_q == 1
reverse_default = "0" if causal or (long_8k and not measured_gqa8k) else "1"
regalloc["reverse_local_assignment"] = os.environ.get(_D128_REVERSE_LOCAL_ENV, reverse_default) == "1"

Earlier optimized performance is the target

We completed PR2709 reproduction before this optimization campaign. The earlier inline assembly implementation achieved 1.0502× speedup against HipKittens on GPU 7.

It won all 50 matched timing pairs. The target is similar performance through PR3843’s native MFMA path.

Wait at the real consumer

An empty tied register pin emits no instruction. The old wait pass waits before that pin.

The changed pass retains pending register scores. It inserts required waits before the next real consumer.

Earlier: LDS load A -> full wait -> empty pin A -> LDS load B -> MFMA
Changed: LDS load A -> empty pin A -> LDS load B -> required wait -> MFMA

The GQA2K loop retains 256 MFMA instructions. Its full LDS waits decrease from 13 to 4.

Explicit completion guards remain. Read the compiler patch. Read the review.

Native dQ completion

Normal LLVM instructions consume dQ through BF16 conversion and packed atomic addition. LLVM models their MFMA dependencies.

The selected MHA1K, MHA2K, MHA4K, and MHA8K paths omit the extra tuple commit.

The machine audits verify the required RAW, WAW, and WAR delays.

Retain the phase completion guard for MHA16K. Its longer test lost 1.30%.

Read the dQ candidate.

Score-panel pipeline

Use MHA2K as the example. Divide the 256 K rows into four 64-row panels.

Each K panel has shape 64×128. The transposed query tile, Q^T, has shape 128×32.

Each score panel has shape 64×32.

Each window computes one score panel and reads the next K panel. The next read does not supply the current calculation.

Ready before the windows: Q^T and K0

Window 0: K0 @ Q^T -> S0    | Read K1
Window 1: K1 @ Q^T -> S1    | Read K2
Window 2: K2 @ Q^T -> S2    | Read K3
Outside:  K3 @ Q^T -> S3

Join S0, S1, S2, S3 in KV-row order.

Each window contains four LDS reads and eight native MFMA instructions. The scheduling masks match the generated ISA.

The longer GPU 7 test measures 730.1 TFLOP/s against a 708.4 TFLOP/s control.

Its matched speedup is 3.13%, with 5/5 timing wins. The earlier optimized MHA2K target remains 751.6 TFLOP/s.

This test uses an isolated compiler with corrected LDS read counts. The current PR does not contain this compiler change.

Current compiler recovery

Beneficial source changes

The final comparison measures the combined source. The following changes address register pressure and scheduling under the current compiler.

Selected techniques and their scope
TechniqueScopeSource change
Native LSE scalingTen measured shapesExpose the FP32 multiply to LLVM. Retain the scalar VGPR identity where selected.
Four-register front pinsSelected BM32 routesUse four-register VGPR groups for scores and dP.
Measured K cacheGQA8K, GQA16K, and MHACache zero low K rows for GQA8K. Cache 64 low K rows for GQA16K and MHA.
Query32 phasesFive measured MHA shapesProcess each outer64 tile in two phases. Keep the existing native MFMA layouts.
Delayed front pinsGQA16K onlyPlace score and dP pins after independent work and before their consumers.
Carried dK fragmentsMeasured fragment routesKeep eight FP32 output fragments across phases. Commit and join them before the final store.

The K cache stores immutable input values. Each phase reloads uncached K rows from LDS when dQ uses them.

The kernel retains native MFMA, persistent result guards, completion boundaries, async waits, and hardware barriers.

These rows do not assign independent percentage gains. Combined changes interact through register allocation and scheduling.

One outer tile: Q rows 0 through 63

Use one dK element, c00=dK[key 0, feature 0]. Every query row adds a contribution to that same output element.

Before: query16 phases                    After: query32 phases

Q rows  0..15 -- contribution 2 --+        Q rows  0..31 -- contributions 2+3 --+
Q rows 16..31 -- contribution 3 --+                                             |
Q rows 32..47 -- contribution 1 --+        Q rows 32..63 -- contributions 1+4 --+
Q rows 48..63 -- contribution 4 --+                                             |
                                |                                             |
c00: 0 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 4 = 10              c00: 0 + (2+3) + (1+4) = 10

Four phase boundaries                    Two phase boundaries
The same 64 query rows                   The same dK output element

The numbers illustrate grouping. They do not describe measured kernel values.

For one native dK fragment, the MFMA instruction uses K=16 in both routes. A query32 phase issues two K16 updates.

query16 phase:  C pin -- MFMA(K16) ------------ D pin
query32 phase:  C pin -- MFMA(K16) -- MFMA(K16) -- D pin

The query32 route retains both matrix updates.
It applies the persistent pin boundary less often.

Both MHA2K loops emit 256 MFMA instructions per outer64 tile. Each contains 192 native16x16x32 and 64 native32x32x16 instructions.

The inspected BM16 loop emits 1,117 instructions. The half-cache BM32 loop emits 1,060 instructions.

Encoded NOP wait states decrease from 131 to 57. Both loops contain zero scratch operations and zero AGPR moves.

Encoded wait states are not elapsed cycles. These two sources differ in tile size and cache design.

Optimization strategy

Optimization techniques and contributions

Use GQA4K as the example: B16, HQ64, HK8, N4096, and D128. A workgroup owns 256 key rows. Each query phase uses 16 query rows.

Each row explains a retained technique and its contribution evidence. These techniques apply to selected noncausal BF16 D128 paths.

Earlier removal tests compare a saved stack with a version that removes the named change. Final extension tests compare the final source with its previous implementation. Shared bundles include several changes. Their results do not isolate each change.

Each speedup uses the geometric mean of matched latency ratios.

Measured shape names refer to the ten configurations in the comparison table.

PR source links identify the rebased implementation. Performance measurements used the campaign compiler.

Running example: carry dK fragments (FRAGMENT_CHAIN)

This example uses noncausal GQA8K with B=16, HQ=64, HK=8, N=8192, D=128, split_q=1.

One workgroup accumulates a 256 × 128 dK tile. Each phase processes 32 query rows.

Wide figures support horizontal scrolling on small screens.

Why different queries update the same output

dK stores the gradient for each key. Different queries use the same key, so their contributions add to that key’s gradient.

Focus on key0, feature0 within this tile. The query index changes, but these output indices stay fixed.

C[key0, feature0] = sum over query rows (
    dS[query, key0] * Q[query, feature0]
)

C is the FP32 accumulator before scaling. The query index is the reduction index, so it does not appear in the output.

The eight query heads in this GQA group share one KV head. Their contributions also add to the same dK tile.

What one phase multiplies

Q0 and Q1 name 32-row query tiles. They do not name individual queries.

For our selected element, phase 0 sums products from query rows 0–31. Phase 1 sums products from query rows 32–63.

The example numbers are illustrative partial sums. They are not Q values, full fragment values, or measured results.

How eight fragments hold the output

The kernel divides the left operand into two logical 128 × 32 blocks. It divides Q into four 32 × 32 feature bands.

The dS and Q operands use BF16. Each fragment accumulates in FP32.

This dK path uses native 32 × 32 × 16 MFMA operations. Each operation updates 32 × 32 outputs using 16 reduction terms.

The compiler combines these operations to cover each 128 × 32 fragment and its 32 query rows.

# Logical update for one fragment in phase p:
c00_next = c00_previous + A0_p @ B0_p

lhs0 and rhs0 hold the current phase’s A0 and B0 operands.

c00 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(
    lhs0, rhs0, c00, accumulator_role="persistent"
)

The third argument contains the previous partial sum. The return value becomes the next phase’s partial sum.

How the partial sum continues across phases

Follow only C[key0, feature0], one element of c00. The full fragment contains 4096 elements.

The vertical line carries the accumulated value. After phase 7, this element includes contributions from query rows 0–255 of the first query head.

Later phases process the remaining query rows and query heads. They continue adding to the same eight fragments.

Total phases = 8 query heads x (8192 query rows / 32 rows per phase)
             = 2048 phases

Eight fragments describe output blocks, not the number of phases. All eight fragments continue through all 2048 phases.

What fragment carry changes

FRAGMENT_CHAIN is a compile-time flag. It keeps the dK fragments separate until all query phases finish.

Each phase updates the eight fragments. Each join below includes the MFMA commit.

With True, the kernel updates the same accumulators across phases. This avoids repeated extraction and joining.

The dK additions follow the same mathematical sequence. The flag changes how the kernel carries accumulators through the loop.

After all phases, the kernel commits and joins the fragments. It applies sm_scale, converts to BF16, and stores dK.

These diagrams describe logical accumulator values. The compiler selects physical registers and layout instructions.

The diagrams describe dK fragment handling. Selected BM16 paths also change dQ handoff scheduling. BM32 retains its dQ commit/preserve boundary.

Timing method and correctness checks

Twenty matched pairs use balanced enabled/disabled and disabled/enabled order. Each graph replay runs eight complete backward calls.

Timing includes accumulator reset, output reset, preprocessing, the main kernel, and dQ conversion. Allocation, forward preparation, compilation, and graph capture occur outside timing.

The inputs share valid FP32 forward state. The scale is 128**-0.5.

Speedup uses the geometric mean of disabled/enabled latency ratios. The latency columns show medians.

The 95% interval from resampling matched pairs is 1.0138–1.0148×. This interval describes one GPU, input seed, and timing session.

TFLOP/s uses 10 × B × HQ × N² × D / (latency_ms × 10⁹).

Both modes pass complete independent FP32 backward checks. All 768 batch/KV-group checks and six global checks pass the 40 dB SNR gate.

Workspace limits and launch protections

Automatic query splitting

Automatic selection starts at 64 initial workgroups or fewer. It targets 256 workgroups. It allows at most 32 splits. It limits partial storage to 64 MiB. It keeps at least four outer iterations per split. Manual splits can use more storage.

Launch protections

Validate accumulator metadata. Use 64-bit pointer rebasing to keep buffer offsets in range. Keep the required copy waits, barriers, and final dQ drain. Preserve exact dispatch and provider fingerprints.

2. Extend dK fragment carry to BM32

Each 32-row query phase updates eight FP32 fragments. Each fragment has 128 rows and 32 columns. Together, they form one 256 × 128 dK tile.

The BM32 baseline commits and joins dK fragments in each phase. The candidate carries these fragments through the phase loop.

After the final dQ drain, commit and join the fragments once. Store the completed dK tile.

Exact values and source pins

Score cache scope: short GQA

Example: One K tile has 256 key rows and 128 contraction columns. Cache the first 64 key rows before the query iterations.

The stream helper uses the cache for GQA lengths 1024, 2048, 4096. These shapes use B=16, HQ=64, HK=8, D=128, noncausal attention, and split 1.

For each 32-column band, the helper uses the cached rows and reads the other 192 key rows from LDS. It preserves all four row blocks and all four 32-column bands. It keeps the score and dP contractions in their original order.

This change extends the score cache technique. The current comparison reports the combined source gain. Historical isolated gains use separate baselines.

Exact stream helper code

Open the candidate source. The listing preserves the exact helper code.

@triton.jit
def _attn_bwd_gqa_front_stream_cache64(
    k_buffer,
    k_score_cache,
    q_t,
    v_operand,
    do_t,
    MMA_NM: tl.constexpr,
    LEFT_LAYOUT: tl.constexpr,
    RIGHT_LAYOUT: tl.constexpr,
):
    """Use cached K rows 0–63 in the original streamed score and dP sequence."""
    tl.static_assert(k_buffer.shape == (256, 128))
    tl.static_assert(k_score_cache.shape == (64, 128))
    tl.static_assert(q_t.shape == (128, 16))
    tl.static_assert(do_t.shape == (128, 16))
    tl.static_assert(v_operand.shape == (256, 128))
    k_score_cache = tlx.require_layout(k_score_cache, LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
    q_t = tlx.require_layout(q_t, RIGHT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
    v_operand = tlx.require_layout(v_operand, LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
    do_t = tlx.require_layout(do_t, RIGHT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
    s0 = tlx.zeros((64, 16), tl.float32, layout=MMA_NM)
    s1 = tlx.zeros((64, 16), tl.float32, layout=MMA_NM)
    s2 = tlx.zeros((64, 16), tl.float32, layout=MMA_NM)
    s3 = tlx.zeros((64, 16), tl.float32, layout=MMA_NM)
    p0 = tlx.zeros((64, 16), tl.float32, layout=MMA_NM)
    p1 = tlx.zeros((64, 16), tl.float32, layout=MMA_NM)
    p2 = tlx.zeros((64, 16), tl.float32, layout=MMA_NM)
    p3 = tlx.zeros((64, 16), tl.float32, layout=MMA_NM)
    for band in tl.static_range(4):
        k0 = tlx.require_layout(tlx.extract_slice(k_score_cache, [64, 32], [0, band * 32]), LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        k1 = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(k_buffer, [64, band * 32], [64, 32]), layout=LEFT_LAYOUT, relaxed=True)
        k2 = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(k_buffer, [128, band * 32], [64, 32]), layout=LEFT_LAYOUT, relaxed=True)
        k3 = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(k_buffer, [192, band * 32], [64, 32]), layout=LEFT_LAYOUT, relaxed=True)
        right_q = tlx.require_layout(tlx.extract_slice(q_t, [32, 16], [band * 32, 0]), RIGHT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        right_do = tlx.require_layout(tlx.extract_slice(do_t, [32, 16], [band * 32, 0]), RIGHT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        left_k = tlx.require_layout(k0, LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        s0 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(left_k, right_q, s0, accumulator_role="transient", initialize=band == 0)
        left_v = tlx.require_layout(tlx.extract_slice(v_operand, [64, 32], [0, band * 32]), LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        p0 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(left_v, right_do, p0, accumulator_role="transient", initialize=band == 0)
        left_k = tlx.require_layout(k1, LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        s1 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(left_k, right_q, s1, accumulator_role="transient", initialize=band == 0)
        left_v = tlx.require_layout(tlx.extract_slice(v_operand, [64, 32], [64, band * 32]), LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        p1 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(left_v, right_do, p1, accumulator_role="transient", initialize=band == 0)
        left_k = tlx.require_layout(k2, LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        s2 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(left_k, right_q, s2, accumulator_role="transient", initialize=band == 0)
        left_v = tlx.require_layout(tlx.extract_slice(v_operand, [64, 32], [128, band * 32]), LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        p2 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(left_v, right_do, p2, accumulator_role="transient", initialize=band == 0)
        left_k = tlx.require_layout(k3, LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        s3 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(left_k, right_q, s3, accumulator_role="transient", initialize=band == 0)
        left_v = tlx.require_layout(tlx.extract_slice(v_operand, [64, 32], [192, band * 32]), LEFT_LAYOUT, pin=False)
        p3 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(left_v, right_do, p3, accumulator_role="transient", initialize=band == 0)
    s_result = tlx.require_layout(tl.cat(tl.cat(s0, s1, dim=0), tl.cat(s2, s3, dim=0), dim=0), MMA_NM, pin=False)
    p_result = tlx.require_layout(tl.cat(tl.cat(p0, p1, dim=0), tl.cat(p2, p3, dim=0), dim=0), MMA_NM, pin=False)
    return s_result, p_result

Combine the fragments after each update

Source lines 1585–1602

    # Complete the independent AGPR chains together before concatenation.
    # Each fresh fragment has one consumer, so post-RA hazard repair can use
    # the actual schedule instead of draining every scheduled MFMA separately.
    c00, c10, c01, c11, c02, c12, c03, c13 = tlx.amd_mfma_commit((c00, c10, c01, c11, c02, c12, c03, c13))

    row0 = tl.cat(
        tl.cat(c00, c01, dim=1),
        tl.cat(c02, c03, dim=1),
        dim=1,
    )
    row1 = tl.cat(
        tl.cat(c10, c11, dim=1),
        tl.cat(c12, c13, dim=1),
        dim=1,
    )
    new_dk = tl.cat(row0, row1, dim=0)
    new_dk = tlx.require_layout(new_dk, MMA_ND, pin=False)
    return new_dk, ds0, ds1

        row0 = tl.cat(tl.cat(c00, c01, dim=1), tl.cat(c02, c03, dim=1), dim=1)
        row1 = tl.cat(tl.cat(c10, c11, dim=1), tl.cat(c12, c13, dim=1), dim=1)
        dk = tlx.require_layout(tl.cat(row0, row1, dim=0), mma_nd, pin=False)

2. Reuse K data and refill consumed Q/dO slices

Noncausal BM16; slice refill follows its selected path

Running example: reuse the K tail

Keep the final 32 key rows in registers across dQ updates. This removes repeated loads from shared memory, called LDS.

Consider one noncausal BM16 workgroup with a 256 × 128 K tile. Each query phase processes 16 query rows.

All K row numbers below are relative to this tile. The K tail contains its final 32 valid rows, numbered 224–255.

Before this optimization, each dQ phase reloaded K rows 224–255 from LDS. K rows 0–223 were already retained in registers.

K-tail reuse: before and after
OperationBeforeAfter
Retain the final K blockRows 192–223; shape 32 × 128Rows 192–255; shape 64 × 128
Get K rows 0–223 in each dQ phaseReuse retained register valuesReuse retained register values
Get rows 224–255 in each dQ phaseLoad them from LDS againExtract them from the retained register value
Get the changing dS bandsLoad them from LDSLoad them from LDS

The optimized path loads all 256 K rows from LDS during initialization. It reuses their register values across dQ phases.

dQ still loads the changing dS bands from LDS. This optimization removes the repeated K-tail load.

Why different query phases use the same K rows

The workgroup keeps its K tile fixed while it processes different query rows. Each phase forms this contribution to dQ:

dQ_phase += SM_SCALE * (dS_phase @ K_tile)

dS_phase: 16 × 256
K_tile:  256 × 128
dQ_phase: 16 × 128

dS_phase holds the gradient of the attention scores for this phase. SM_SCALE is the attention scale.

The query rows and dS_phase change between phases. K stays fixed.

For example, the phases for query rows 0–15 and 16–31 both need K[230].

Before, each dQ phase loads that row from LDS. After, both phases use its retained register value.

Read the extract_slice arguments

k7 = tlx.extract_slice(
    k_resident_band6,
    [32, 128],  # Slice size.
    [32, 0],    # Slice offset.
)

[32, 128] gives the slice size. [32, 0] gives its offset within k_resident_band6.

The retained block starts at K row 192. Offset 32 therefore selects row 192 + 32 = 224.

The slice contains rows 224–255. This operation extracts existing register values without another LDS load.

The causal branch retains 32 rows and keeps the LDS load for k7.

Retained K block · K-tail extraction and causal fallback

Performance tradeoff

Fewer LDS loads can reduce memory instructions and load dependencies. Additional live K values can increase register pressure.

The compiler determines physical register allocation and any spills.

Historical GQA4K component tests measured 1.01638× speedup, approximately 1.64%, with 5/5 paired wins.

The 1.0441× result also includes Q/dO slice refill. These measurements describe their archived sources and shapes.

Historical component measurements · K-tail and slice-refill bundle

Running example: refill consumed Q/dO slices

Archived noncausal BM16 schedule with continuous delayed dQ

Both versions compute the same gradients. The change starts future Q/dO copies earlier.

Q contains query values. dO contains the gradient of the attention output.

Each phase updates dK and dV for its current 16 query rows. Later phases also compute delayed dQ contributions from the previous phase's dS.

This example starts with T0: query rows 0–63. Each phase reads a 16 × 128 slice of both Q and dO.

Buffer 0 holds T0. Buffer 1 already holds T1: query rows 64–127.

Buffer 0 next receives T2: query rows 128–191. outer_step + 2 selects this future tile for the same buffer slot.

Arrows mark copy starts after the phase-end barrier. Each copy can remain in flight during later computation.

P contains attention probabilities. dP contains their gradient. dS contains the gradient of the attention scores.

P0 skips the initial zero dQ contribution. T1's P0 later computes the dQ contribution for T0's P3.

The S0 copy can run while P1 computes dK, dV, and P0's delayed dQ. The original full-tile copy could also overlap T1 computation.

The phase-end barrier ensures all readers finish before a copy overwrites their slice.

Copy waits and barriers ensure future data is ready before the kernel uses the buffer again.

Phase 3 also refills the 64-row LSE and Delta statistics after all four phases finish their reads.

Phase-end reader barrier · Slice copy and outer_step + 2 · Copy wait and buffer boundary

A phase completes its shared-memory reads before the next Q/dO slice copy starts.

3. Interleave score and dP calculations

Noncausal BM16 GQA front

The GQA4K front alternates independent score and dP matrix operations.

Each accumulation chain keeps ascending 32-column bands.

This source order gives the compiler independent work between dependent updates.

Running example: interleave score and dP calculations

Alternate score updates and dP updates to expose independent work between dependent accumulation steps.

Consider one phase with 16 query rows, 256 keys, and 128 features.

Q and dO each have shape 16 × 128. K and V each have shape 256 × 128.

The code computes two independent matrix products in a transposed output layout:

score_product_T = K_tile @ Q_slice.T    # Shape: 256 x 16.
dP_T            = V_tile @ dO_slice.T   # Shape: 256 x 16.

The kernel applies the attention scale to the score product later.

dP depends on dO and V. It does not require the attention probabilities P.

The kernel combines P and dP later to calculate the score gradient dS.

Split the 128 features into four bands

Each matrix product sums contributions across 128 features. Each band contains 32 feature columns from the same query phase.

The four feature bands
BandFeature columns
B00–31
B132–63
B264–95
B396–127

Focus on one 64-key group within this phase.

In the diagram, S[B0] updates a score accumulator using B0. D[B0] updates a dP accumulator using B0.

Why interleaving can help

  • S[B1] needs the accumulator result from S[B0].
  • D[B0] uses a separate accumulator.
  • The compiler can schedule independent dP work between dependent score updates.

MFMA is AMD's matrix multiply-accumulate instruction. More independent updates can reduce waits for previous MFMA results.

Each accumulator still processes B0, B1, B2, B3 in order. The change alters the order of independent updates.

Read the eight accumulators in the code

The helper uses four score accumulators and four dP accumulators. Each accumulator has shape 64 × 16.

The pairs are s0/p0, s1/p1, s2/p2, and s3/p3. Each pair covers 64 keys and all 16 query rows.

The variables p0 through p3 hold partial dP values.

Source order within each feature band:

  s0 -> p0 -> s1 -> p1 -> s2 -> p2 -> s3 -> p3

  s0/p0: keys   0-63
  s1/p1: keys  64-127
  s2/p2: keys 128-191
  s3/p3: keys 192-255

Repeat this order for B0, B1, B2, B3.

Separate score product · Separate dP product · Interleaved MFMA updates

Read the measured scope

Historical GQA4K tests measured 1.0187× speedup and 5/5 paired wins for the score/dP and delayed-dQ handoff bundle.

The report assigns no separate speedup to score/dP interleaving.

def _attn_bwd_gqa_dkdv_braid_prefetch(

):

    tl.static_assert(dv_rhs.shape == (16, 128))

    dv_rhs = tlx.require_layout(dv_rhs, Q_OUT_LAYOUT, pin=False)

    kl0 = tlx.extract_slice(dk_lhs, [128, 16], [0, 0])

    vl1 = tlx.extract_slice(dv_lhs, [128, 16], [128, 0])
    k00, k10, k01, k11, k02, k12, k03, k13 = dk
    kr0 = tlx.extract_slice(dk_rhs, [16, 32], [0, 0])
    vr0 = tlx.extract_slice(dv_rhs, [16, 32], [0, 0])

    v00 = tlx.extract_slice(dv, [128, 32], [0, 0])
    k10 = tlx.require_layout(k10, MMA_ND, pin=False)
    v10 = tlx.extract_slice(dv, [128, 32], [128, 0])
    kr1 = tlx.extract_slice(dk_rhs, [16, 32], [0, 32])
    vr1 = tlx.extract_slice(dv_rhs, [16, 32], [0, 32])
    k01 = tlx.require_layout(k01, MMA_ND, pin=False)
    v01 = tlx.extract_slice(dv, [128, 32], [0, 32])
    k11 = tlx.require_layout(k11, MMA_ND, pin=False)
    v11 = tlx.extract_slice(dv, [128, 32], [128, 32])
    kr2 = tlx.extract_slice(dk_rhs, [16, 32], [0, 64])
    vr2 = tlx.extract_slice(dv_rhs, [16, 32], [0, 64])
    k02 = tlx.require_layout(k02, MMA_ND, pin=False)
    v02 = tlx.extract_slice(dv, [128, 32], [0, 64])
    k12 = tlx.require_layout(k12, MMA_ND, pin=False)
    v12 = tlx.extract_slice(dv, [128, 32], [128, 64])
    kr3 = tlx.extract_slice(dk_rhs, [16, 32], [0, 96])
    vr3 = tlx.extract_slice(dv_rhs, [16, 32], [0, 96])
    k03 = tlx.require_layout(k03, MMA_ND, pin=False)
    v03 = tlx.extract_slice(dv, [128, 32], [0, 96])
    k13 = tlx.require_layout(k13, MMA_ND, pin=False)
    v13 = tlx.extract_slice(dv, [128, 32], [128, 96])
    v00 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(vl0, vr0, v00, accumulator_role="transient")
    v10 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(vl1, vr0, v10, accumulator_role="transient")
    k00 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(kl0, kr0, k00, accumulator_role="persistent")
    k10 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(kl1, kr0, k10, accumulator_role="persistent")
    ds0 = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(prev_ds, [0, 0], [16, 32]), layout=DS_MD_LAYOUT, relaxed=True)
    v01 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(vl0, vr1, v01, accumulator_role="transient")
    v11 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(vl1, vr1, v11, accumulator_role="transient")
    k01 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(kl0, kr1, k01, accumulator_role="persistent")
    k11 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(kl1, kr1, k11, accumulator_role="persistent")
    v02 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(vl0, vr2, v02, accumulator_role="transient")
    v12 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(vl1, vr2, v12, accumulator_role="transient")
    k02 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(kl0, kr2, k02, accumulator_role="persistent")
    k12 = tlx.amd_scheduled_mfma(kl1, kr2, k12, accumulator_role="persistent")
    ds1 = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(prev_ds, [0, 32], [16, 32]), layout=DS_MD_LAYOUT, relaxed=True)

    return (k00, k10, k01, k11, k02, k12, k03, k13), new_dv, ds0, ds1

Exact GQA fragment regression tests

Both exact signatures passed on 12 October 2026: (16,64,8,8192,128) and (15,64,8,16384,128).

The cases use BF16, noncausal attention, split_q=1, and sm_scale=1/16.

Q band weights use (1,2,16,32). K and dO band weights retain (1,2,4,8).

All eight dK reference fragments are distinct. Each case checks all 28 fragment pairs with the 1% pointwise tolerance.

The c00/c12 and c01/c13 pairs now differ. Nonzero entries differ by at least 50% within every pair.

Each case also checks the compiled fragment state and the final query rows.

Pointwise checks use 1% relative tolerance and zero absolute tolerance. Global SNR must reach 40 dB.

Tile checks require 40 dB for every 16-row dQ group and every 64-row dK group.

The two numerical cases and eight dispatch guards passed. No case skipped. These checks extend the earlier 101-test validation.

Measure each technique within the archived stack

Each comparison runs the frozen baseline against a version with one change removed.

A positive paired gain favors the frozen baseline. A negative paired gain favors the removal version.

These measurements describe contribution within the archived stack. They do not recreate the original optimization order.

The earlier accepted-stack results remain historical comparisons. A current-minus-one result can differ from the earlier optimization result.

Do not add these percentages. Techniques can affect each other through register use, instruction order, and selected kernel paths.

Saved time is the difference between latency medians.

The paired gain uses the geometric mean of five paired latency ratios.

Archived baseline source b6288dd2b179 · Timing device BDF 0000:e5:00.0

All configurations use BF16, D128, noncausal attention, and split 1.

1K = 1024 query rows. GQA4K uses B16, Hq64, Hkv8, N4096, and D128.

GQA16K uses B15, Hq64, Hkv8, N16384, and D128.

Timings and same-source controls used 0000:e5:00.0.

Numerical tests of these sources and shapes used 0000:65:00.0.

Both devices use gfx950.

The numerical tests did not run on the timing device.

Timing uses GPU E5. Numerical qualification covers the source and shapes on GPU65. It does not establish numerical accuracy on GPU E5.

Read the measured outcomes

The 63 initial comparisons contain 41 current gains, 13 inconclusive results, 2 removal gains, and 7 unqualified results.

The BM32 route gives the largest measured gain.

GQA 8K gains +16.75% with the BM32 route.

GQA 16K gains +9.39% with the BM32 route.

Compiler settings reach +8.91% at GQA 16K.

T4 has no clear positive gain.

MHA8K runs faster when K-tail reuse is removed in the component comparison.

MHA8K also runs faster when zero-dQ omission is removed in the T4 comparison.

Slice refill retained a +2.81% gain at MHA8K.

Its initial +6.01% magnitude did not reproduce.

The initial +3.69% final-copy result did not reproduce.

The +0.04% repeat remained inconclusive.

The initial final-copy value does not establish a stable performance benefit.

Keep dependencies visible

The BM32 removal selects the existing BM16 route. It also removes access to the GQA16K early-operand bridge.

This result measures the BM32 route as a group of changes. It does not isolate query tile size.

GQA16K zero-dQ omission, the phase-0 IGLP2 hint, and final-copy suppression also differ between the BM32 and BM16 routes.

The final-refill variant retains the peeled final step. It restores the two final slice copies.

Technique 6 removal restores reverse local assignment off for every shape. It preserves the technique 9 MHA16K sinking default.

Native comparison can show the same main instructions and resource descriptor. It also checks the LDS size.

Such a result has no separate attributed gain.

What each removal changes
  1. 1. Carry dK fragments.

    Keep eight dK fragments through the query loop. The removal variant combines dK after each phase.

    Measured scope. GQA1K, GQA2K, GQA4K, and all five MHA configurations use this comparison.

    Dependencies. The source avoids repeated dK assembly between phases. The removal preserves short-GQA interleave, transient dQ selection, and zero-dQ omission.

  2. 2. Reuse K and refill slices.

    Keep the final 32 K rows in registers. Copy consumed Q/dO slices before the next use. Separate variants restore K-tail loads and full-slot refill.

    Measured scope. GQA1K, GQA2K, GQA4K, and all five MHA configurations use the BM16 path.

    Dependencies. This source reduces K loads from LDS and starts Q/dO copies earlier. The comparison preserves the required slot ownership, waits, and barriers. Keeping K rows in registers extends their lifetimes. This can change register pressure and scheduling. These potential effects do not establish the cause of a timing loss.

  3. 3. Interleave score and dP.

    Alternate independent score and dP chains. The removal variant completes score before dP.

    Measured scope. GQA1K, GQA2K, and GQA4K use this comparison.

    Dependencies. The source exposes independent matrix chains to the scheduler. Each chain keeps ascending K32 bands and the same operands.

  4. 4. Omit initial zero dQ.

    Remove the first known-zero dQ operation. The removal variant restores its matrix operation and atomic update.

    Measured scope. GQA1K, GQA2K, GQA4K, GQA16K, and all five MHA configurations use this comparison.

    Dependencies. This change requires the previous dS tile to be zero. The removal retains the zero seed, dQ reset, and final drain.

  5. 5. Use the BM32 route.

    Use the 32-row route for long GQA. The removal variant selects the existing BM16 route.

    Measured scope. GQA8K and GQA16K use the BM32 path. The final-copy component applies to GQA16K.

    Dependencies. At GQA16K, the BM16 route also removes early dQ preparation, zero-dQ omission, phase-0 IGLP2, and final-copy suppression.

  6. 6. Select compiler settings.

    Shape defaults control reverse local assignment and instruction sinking. GQA16K also uses phase-0 amd_iglp_opt(2). Separate variants remove register defaults and the instruction hint.

    Measured scope. The combined comparison covers all ten configurations. The separate register-default and instruction-hint components cover GQA16K.

    Dependencies. The removal keeps MHA16K sinking off for technique 9. The instruction-hint component requires the BM32 GQA16K route. The comparison retains regclass_priority_trumps_globalness unchanged. Its default is False.

  7. 7. Prepare dQ operands.

    Prepare future dS/K operands before the next dQ matrix operation. The removal variant selects the prior bridge.

    Measured scope. GQA16K uses this comparison. Its query/KV head ratio is 8.

    Dependencies. This change requires the BM32 route. The comparison preserves ascending K32 bands and the existing dQ atomic updates.

  8. 8. Interleave dK and dV.

    Alternate independent short-GQA feature bands. The removal variant completes dV before dK.

    Measured scope. GQA2K and GQA4K use this comparison. Their query/KV head ratio is 8.

    Dependencies. The source exposes independent dK and dV chains. The comparison keeps the dK representation and each output’s query accumulation order.

  9. 9. Disable MHA16K sinking.

    Disable instruction sinking for the exact MHA16K shape. The removal variant enables instruction sinking.

    Measured scope. The exact shape is B16, Hq16, Hkv16, N16384, and D128.

Archived baseline kernel · Source b6288dd2b179

Notation

B is batch size. Hq and Hkv count query and KV heads. N is query and KV length.

D is head dimension. dQ, dK, and dV are the query, key, and value gradients.

MFMA multiplies matrices and accumulates results. LDS is shared memory within a GPU block.

dP is the probability gradient. dS is the score gradient. Delta uses the supplied O and dO values.

Throughput uses 10 × B × Hq × N² × D / (latency_ms × 10⁹).

Archived status statements describe their recorded validation dates. Read current production validation for the promoted 82aeae06 source.

Each archived result keeps its original date, source, control, and qualification scope.

Change only the MHA16K dQ accumulator

For example, shape 9 has 64 key tiles. Current sends all 64 partial results to one BF16 dQ plane.

Grouped2 sends tiles 0–31 to plane 0 and tiles 32–63 to plane 1. Each plane still uses BF16 atomics.

The converter adds both plane values in FP32 and rounds once to BF16. dQ storage increases from 1 GiB to 2 GiB.

The query split remains 1. This change does not reduce the total number of atomic additions.

See the one-plane workflow, two-plane workflow, and existing code examples: allocation, plane selection, BF16 atomics, and FP32 merge.

Reuse the first 64 K rows

The candidate holds the first 64 K rows in registers. It loads the other 192 K rows from LDS.

The helper joins these rows in their original order. It performs one score dot across all 128 features.

The helper uses K[256,128] and Qᵀ[128,16]. It produces Score[256,16].

Before: current grouped2

  1. Allocate and reset two dQ planes2 GiB; outside event timing.
  2. Compute DeltaSum O × dO over 128 features.
  3. Compute the gradientsRead all 256 K rows from LDS for the score operand.
  4. Convert dQCombine both planes and return dQ, dK, and dV.

After: cache64 candidate

  1. Allocate and reset two dQ planes2 GiB; outside event timing.
  2. Compute DeltaThe preprocessing kernel remains unchanged.
  3. Compute the gradientsReuse 64 K rows and load 192 K rows from LDS.
  4. Convert dQThe converter remains unchanged.

Check the native cost

Native code contains 28 fewer ds_read_b128 instructions. This count does not measure runtime stalls.

The total VGPR and AGPR count rises from 498 to 510. LDS remains 153,888 bytes, with zero scratch and occupancy 1.

Both versions use a 2 GiB dQ accumulator. This candidate adds no accumulator storage.

Exact helper code
@triton.jit
def _attn_bwd_mha_score_cache64(
    k_buffer,
    k_score_cache,
    q_t,
    MMA_NM: tl.constexpr,
    K_NM_LAYOUT: tl.constexpr,
):
    """Keep native K ownership through ordered joins before one full score dot."""
    tl.static_assert(k_buffer.shape == (256, 128))
    tl.static_assert(k_score_cache.shape == (64, 128))
    tl.static_assert(q_t.shape == (128, 16))
    k0 = tlx.require_layout(k_score_cache, K_NM_LAYOUT, pin=True)
    k1 = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(k_buffer, [64, 0], [64, 128]), layout=K_NM_LAYOUT, relaxed=True)
    k1 = tlx.require_layout(k1, K_NM_LAYOUT, pin=True)
    k2 = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(k_buffer, [128, 0], [64, 128]), layout=K_NM_LAYOUT, relaxed=True)
    k2 = tlx.require_layout(k2, K_NM_LAYOUT, pin=True)
    k3 = tlx.local_load(tlx.local_slice(k_buffer, [192, 0], [64, 128]), layout=K_NM_LAYOUT, relaxed=True)
    k3 = tlx.require_layout(k3, K_NM_LAYOUT, pin=True)
    k01 = tlx.require_layout(tl.cat(k0, k1, can_reorder=False, dim=0), K_NM_LAYOUT, pin=True)
    k23 = tlx.require_layout(tl.cat(k2, k3, can_reorder=False, dim=0), K_NM_LAYOUT, pin=True)
    k_nm = tlx.require_layout(tl.cat(k01, k23, can_reorder=False, dim=0), K_NM_LAYOUT, pin=True)
    return tl.dot(k_nm, q_t, tlx.zeros((256, 16), tl.float32, layout=MMA_NM))

Extra events and host launch wrappers can change the measured intervals.

A stage interval can include a host submission gap. It does not measure only GPU instruction time.

Keep the two difference calculations separate

The unpaired difference of medians subtracts the composite latency median from the current latency median.

The median paired difference first subtracts each matched round. It then takes the median of five round differences.

Positive values indicate shorter composite intervals. Negative values indicate longer composite intervals.

These calculations can give different values or signs.

Divide the dQ accumulator by key tile

The converter adds both planes in FP32 and writes BF16 dQ.

Exact code for the storage change

Allocate two planes for the selected configuration

The dispatch selects two planes only for this noncausal MHA16K configuration with split 1.

def _allocate_dq_accumulator(q, k, causal=False, split_q=None):
    """Allocate the exact storage contract selected by the D128 dispatch."""
    shape = (q.shape[0], q.shape[1], k.shape[1], q.shape[2], q.shape[3])
    dispatch = _select_d128_interleaved_dispatch(shape, causal, split_q)
    if dispatch.convert_entry is _attn_bwd_dq_native_planes2_convert_kernel:
        return torch.zeros((2, *q.shape), device=q.device, dtype=q.dtype)
    return torch.zeros_like(q)
Select the plane from the key tile

pid_n identifies the key tile.

BLOCK_N=256 gives 64 key tiles and 32 tiles per plane.

The pointer offset uses 64-bit arithmetic.

    if BATCH == 16 and HQ == 16 and HK == 16 and N == 16384 and not IS_CAUSAL and SPLIT_Q == 1:
        dq_plane = (pid_n // (N // BLOCK_N // 2)).to(tl.int64)
        DQ_ACC = DQ_ACC + dq_plane * BATCH * HQ * N * D
    DQ_ACC = DQ_ACC + q_batch_base
Add BF16 partial dQ values

Merge both planes in FP32

The converter reads both BF16 planes.

It adds their values in FP32 before the final BF16 store.

    values = tlx.buffer_load(DQ_ACC, native_offsets, contiguity=4).to(tl.float32)

    # Preserve the existing logical output layout contract.
    values = tlx.require_layout(values, store_layout, pin=True)

    store_m = tile_m_base + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)

    tl.store(DQ + store_offsets, values.to(tl.bfloat16))

9. Disable instruction sinking for MHA16K

B16, Hq16, Hkv16, N16384, D128; noncausal; split 1

The exact MHA16K default disables instruction sinking.

Reverse local assignment remains enabled.

The guard keeps other shapes, causal attention, and split 2 on their previous defaults.

Five pairs improved against prior TLX and HipKittens.

Before

reverse_default = "0" if causal or long_8k else "1"
sink_default = "0" if short_gqa or long_8k else "1"
regalloc["reverse_local_assignment"] = os.environ.get(_D128_REVERSE_LOCAL_ENV, reverse_default) == "1"
regalloc["sink_insts_to_avoid_spills"] = os.environ.get(_D128_SINK_INSTS_ENV, sink_default) == "1"

After

reverse_default = "0" if causal or long_8k else "1"
sink_default = "0" if (short_gqa or long_8k or (
        shape == (16, 16, 16, 16384, 128) and not causal and split_q == 1
    )) else "1"
regalloc["reverse_local_assignment"] = os.environ.get(_D128_REVERSE_LOCAL_ENV, reverse_default) == "1"
regalloc["sink_insts_to_avoid_spills"] = os.environ.get(_D128_SINK_INSTS_ENV, sink_default) == "1"
